result:
I want to write about the way a city forgets to be loud at 4:17 a.m.

It’s the hour between the last bus and the first delivery truck. The streetlights hum, but they don’t glare. Everything is rinsed in that thin, blue-grey light that makes buildings look like they’re made of wet paper.

I was on my balcony with a mug that had gone cold. Below me, a woman in a yellow raincoat was walking a dog that didn’t want to walk. She kept stopping to let it sniff the same drain grate. The dog was serious about it. She was serious about letting it be serious. No one was watching. That was the point.

It made me think about how much of life is just maintenance for other people’s stories. We are the background characters in a hundred small narratives we’ll never know. The barista who remembers my order. The neighbor who always takes the trash cans in on Tuesdays. The guy who waters the planters outside the laundromat even though no one asked him to.

And yet at 4:17 a.m., all of that falls away. The roles thin out. You are just a warm body in the dark, listening to the radiator tick.

I used to think freedom was a big, dramatic thing. A plane ticket. A resignation letter. A new haircut in a new town. Now I think it’s smaller. It’s the permission to stand still for a minute and not produce anything. To watch a dog sniff a drain grate and not turn it into a metaphor.

There’s a kid two floors down who practices violin at night. It’s terrible, in the best way. He’s learning. He hits the same wrong note every time, then corrects it, then hits it again. He’s been doing that for weeks. I’ve never heard it resolve. Maybe it never will. Maybe that’s the song.

I finished my cold coffee and went back inside. The apartment was quiet. The refrigerator kicked on. Somewhere, a train sighed.

Freedom, I think, is not having to be the one who writes the story down. Sometimes you can just be the person who notices the light on the kitchen counter at 7 a.m. and decides that’s enough for today.
